extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, art students, and art critics interested in Gothic art and general principles of artistic truth and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for judging or producing painting, sculpture, and Gothic architecture—focusing on truthfulness (naturalism), composition (design), moral selection of subject, and treatment of detail. Includes examples of common errors and guidance on balance between imitation and invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men of facts envying design (imitative error)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When, having only imitative powers, they refuse to employ those powers upon the visible world around them; but, having been taught that composition is the end of art, strive to obtain the inventive powers which nature has denied them, study nothing but the works of reputed designers, and perish in a fungous growth of plagiarism and laws of art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is condemned as a great error: artists who copy other designers instead of studying nature become useless, producing base resemblances of truth or fancy. Avoid learning art only from other designers; study the visible world and develop original composition from observed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men of design envying facts (over‑imitation of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the temptation of closely imitating nature leads them to forget their own proper ornamental function, and when they lose the power of the composition for the sake of graphic truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the desire to make an ornament or composition look indistinguishable from its natural model override the work’s ornamental or compositional purpose (example: hawthorn moulding painted green). Designers must preserve their formal function rather than slavishly copying surface appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of fact and design (central class ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists of the central or greatest class “possess the powers of both” — they perceive and pursue both good and evil together and render the whole thing as it is; Gothic builders are held to be of this class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for both faithful observation of facts and strong compositional invention. The ideal art of Gothic builders combines truthful rendering with disciplined design; neither faculty should be neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of veracity / truthfulness in representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic characteristic is an “intense love of veracity” — rendering external and imaginative truth as faithfully as possible (e.g., making a purgatorial fire “as like real fire as he can”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value accurate, truthful depiction of natural and symbolic subjects; employ detailed, honest observation. But temper veracity with thought — truthful detail should serve meaning and design rather than become mere display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid thoughtless surface truth; seek inner meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The love of truth can err “by seizing on a surface truth instead of an inner one” (example: literal imitation of flame may miss symbolizing unquenchableness and divine wrath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rendering symbols or phenomena, ask what inward quality or moral meaning must be conveyed. Do not mistake faithful mimicry of appearance for full truthful expression; prioritize the inner truth the work ought to communicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism — represent the whole of nature (balanced portraiture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalism is described as taking “all” of nature and making one harmony of it; it enables the representation of the full range of human passions and the varieties of leaves and branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to represent subjects in their wholeness—strengths and faults alike—with balance of color and chiaroscuro. Naturalist work should not idealize away human or natural imperfection but incorporate it into an overall nobility or truthful harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Sensualism (delighting in evil or degradation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sensualist “perceive[s] and imitate[s] evil only… delight in the beggary and brutality of the human race… their colour is… lurid… greatest spaces... occupied by darkness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depict vice, misery, or repulsive detail merely for excitement or aesthetic shock. Works portraying evil or suffering should have moral purpose or higher meaning; gratuitous or celebratory vulgarity is condemned (examples: certain beggar scenes and delight in filthy detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purists — select and exalt the good; appropriate idealization
rubrics_metrics.description: Purists “take the good and leave the evil… gather what [nature] has of grace, and life, and light, and holiness, and leave all… of the rest undrawn.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is devotional or ideal, legitimately emphasize the good and dignified aspects of the subject. Healthy Purism elevates heart and character while avoiding crude smoothing that disguises truth; but beware vulgar Purism that rejects truth out of false fastidiousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of act / moral selection of details
rubrics_metrics.description: On selection of incidents and details: the artist should choose acts that give moral or sympathetic interest (critique of Murillo’s beggar boys: the painter delights in disgusting manner of eating rather than creating sympathy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer moments or poses that elicit the intended response (charity, pity, reverence). Avoid choosing details simply to display technical skill or grossness (e.g., exhibiting the sole of a foot to show dust) when they add nothing to the lesson or moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of sight — avoid shortness of sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Naturalists and Purists “may err from shortness of sight, from not seeing all that there is in nature; seeing only the outsides of things” (example: a continental Naturalist sees anatomy but not the color against the sky).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate penetration, sympathy, and imagination to perceive depth (color, light relationships, inner character) rather than fixating on superficial facts. Avoid vulgar Naturalism or Purism that brings discredit by narrow observation or silly choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetation and foliage as legitimate subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic workmen displayed a “peculiar fondness for the forms of Vegetation,” struggling “to render all its characters with as much accuracy as was compatible with the laws of his design and the nature of his material.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study plant forms closely and render foliage with truthful variety, while still respecting overall composition and material constraints. Prefer realistic foliage to conventional, lifeless ornament when it serves the work’s character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject conventional, lifeless ornament in favor of natural forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast with Greek/Roman/Byzantine conventional foliage: “The Gothic sculptor… could not rest in [conventional types]… he put more of nature into his work, until at last it was all true.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor truthful, lively forms over stylized, sterile conventions when they help convey vitality. Yet integration with disciplined arrangement remains necessary; naturalism should be compatible with design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest portraiture — record virtues and faults without exaltation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic sculpture gives “what kingliness and sanctity was in them, to the full, mixed with due record of their faults… with a great indifference like that of Scripture history.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray subjects (kings, saints, common people) honestly—neither inflating them into demi-gods nor excusing failings. Leave moral judgment to the viewer when appropriate; maintain equitable and minute delineation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of everyday life and domestic detail as meaningful record
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic sculpture and painting are “full of valuable portraiture of the greatest men, but copious records of all the domestic customs and inferior arts of the ages in which it flourished.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ familiar, domestic, and occupational details to enrich narrative, symbolism, and historical record. These particulars should illuminate the scene’s meaning rather than function as mere antiquarian curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of color and chiaroscuro to express moral/affective range
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists of the central class render subjects whose “color [is] equally balanced between splendor and sadness” and whose “chiaroscuro [is] equally balanced between light and shade.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color and light/shade deliberately to express the coexistence of good and evil, joy and sorrow. Technical choices in color and chiaroscuro should support the work’s moral and emotional complexity rather than flattening it into one tone.
